extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political theory, statesmen, and lawmakers interested in constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative principles and standards for what makes stable, good constitutions and forms of government (mixed government, separation of powers, checks, magistracy design), illustrated by historical municipal examples (e.g., Pistoia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentration of all authority in one assembly
rubrics_metrics.description: Here again is a constitution of all authority in one assembly. The council of an hundred was sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adams criticizes systems where legislative, executive, and judicial powers are collected in a single popular assembly because that concentration produces capricious, tempestuous government and factional violence; decisions should be subject to checks and not rest solely with one sovereign assembly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division / separation of powers (mixed constitution)
rubrics_metrics.description: All authority, legislative, executive, and judicial, was collected together in one single assembly ... we contend [against government concentrated in one centre].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A stable constitution divides authority among different magistracies and bodies (e.g., consuls, podesta, councils) so that no single organ can act unchecked; Adams favors mixed government forms that balance popular and elite elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective checks and negatives (vetoes) to prevent majority tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: The confuls ... had no negative upon any deliberation or resolution of the great council: and, on the other hand, the people had no negative, not even the poor protection of a tribunitian veto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutions should provide institutional negatives or veto powers (tribunician or executive negatives) to prevent rash or oppressive majoritarian measures; absence of such checks breeds faction and instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vesting whole judicial + executive power in one official
rubrics_metrics.description: In this magistrate was vested the whole judicial power, both in private and criminal causes, and in those which were public and criminal; and therefore the podesta was the ordinary judge in the city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrating military/administrative/judicial authority in a single magistrate (e.g., podesta) undermines rule of law and accountability; judicial functions should be insulated from executive command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent rotation / short terms of magistrates
rubrics_metrics.description: These twelve magistrates [anziani] were renewed every two months; and afterwards, as appears by a law of 1277, it was established that the anzianate should not continue longer than one month.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, frequently-rotated terms prevent accumulation of power and corruption but can create instability and lack of continuity; term length must balance accountability and effective governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sortition / lottery/drawing for selecting officials
rubrics_metrics.description: They made eight purses ... After the oaths of office shall be taken, they shall cause nine votes, with their names, to be put into a purse by a notary, one of which shall be drawn out for a president, and so successively during the term of their office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Random selection (drawing from lots/purses) for certain offices is advocated as a device to curb faction, patronage, and oligarchic capture, but must be combined with other checks for competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction or control of aristocratic grandees
rubrics_metrics.description: By the laws of the years 1330 and 1344, to be declared a grandee was rather an infamy than an honour ... they were excluded entirely from all magistracies and offices, and subjected to penalties still more rigorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutions should include mechanisms to restrain elites who abuse power (e.g., exclusion from office, penalties) to protect the public peace and prevent oligarchic domination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment of foreigners or outsiders to certain offices to reduce local faction
rubrics_metrics.description: The election of this ruler was to be made by the anziani, in the person of some foreigner, and not of any citizen of Pistoia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting a foreigner or non-local for key magistracies (podesta, captain) can reduce factional interests and partiality, but raises issues of responsiveness and accountability to local citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magistrates and councils must be bound by laws and statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: They began ... to make their proper statutes, and establish their popular government ... and all laws, resolutions, and deliberations, first proposed and digested in the smaller council, by the few, must be here confirmed or rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional design requires clear statutes and procedural rules for proposing, deliberating, and confirming laws so that ad hoc authority is constrained and decisions are deliberative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation by balanced local constituencies (quarter/ward representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The council of an hundred ... elected in the proportion of five and twenty for each of the four gates or quarters of the city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation should reflect local subdivisions and balance geographic or guild-based interests to prevent domination by a single quarter or class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent audit / accounting and accountability of magistrates
rubrics_metrics.description: The city of Pistoia had also in its regimen a syndick. This was an officer ... His duty was to look over the accounts of the podesta, the captain of the people, the anziani, and all the magistrates and officers of the city and its district, when they resigned or were dismissed from their charges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Financial oversight institutions (syndic, auditors) are essential to accountability; officials must render accounts on leaving office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia as civic defense and instrument of public order (not permanent private armies)
rubrics_metrics.description: The city thought it necessary to create certain companies of armed men ... These companies were called ... the Equestrian and Pedestrian Orders ... each company had two captains, one gonfalonier ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citizen militias organized under civil magistracy can be used to support public order and the enforcement of laws; constitutional design must regulate military force to prevent its capture by factions or magnates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong penalties and public enforcement against elite violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon the commission of any homicide [by a grandee], to draw forth the standard of justice ... to cause his goods to be destroyed, and not to suffer the said standard to repose, until all the property of such delinquent shall be totally destroyed and laid waste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harsh public penalties and uncompromising enforcement against powerful offenders were used historically to deter aristocratic impunity; modern constitutions should ensure impartial enforcement of criminal law regardless of rank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sumptuary and moral regulation to preserve public order
rubrics_metrics.description: They also superintended the sumptuary laws, against all luxurious excesses in the dress and ornaments of the ladies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations of luxury and public morality were seen as instruments to maintain civic virtue and social order; constitutional frameworks often interact with cultural/legal norms to shape behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve municipal liberties while acknowledging higher sovereignty where necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: This concession of governing themselves by their own laws, obtained by the provinces of Italy, was the mere liberality of Charlemagne ... reserving always, nevertheless, the sovereignty to their lords.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local self-government must be designed in light of feudal or imperial overlordship; constitutions should clearly define the limits of municipal autonomy and the reserved rights of higher sovereigns to avoid conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rapid, extensive constitutional innovation that destroys stability
rubrics_metrics.description: To such extremes of caprice and violence, destructive of all liberty and safety, are such governments naturally and necessarily reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent radical reforms or abrupt institutional changes (faction-driven reforms) can create caprice and violence; gradual, well-deliberated constitutional alterations preserve order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of magistracies: distinct roles for executive, judicial, and military functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The podesta, consuls, council of an hundred, and rectors of the chapels and arts, were all collected in one assembly, to determine on grants for money, peace, war, truce, alliance, &c. and all questions were determined by the vote of the majority, which necessarily made that tempestuous and capricious government in one centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutions should assign distinct competencies to magistracies (finance, war, justice) rather than collect them in a single body; overlapping or conflated roles lead to instability and abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of term-limited, oath-bound offices with attendant counselors to limit arbitrary power
rubrics_metrics.description: To the podesta, for his regulation in the exercise of his office, were given by the city fourteen counsellors, and two judges ... and by the opinion of all these he decided upon those things which affected the honour or utility of the public, as he himself, after having made his election of these attendants, was obliged to stand by their advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term limits, formal oaths, and institutionalized advisory councils restrain single-officer arbitrariness and tie decisions to collective judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of magistrates via mixed procedures (election + intervention of guilds/arts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The election of these magistrates was made every year by the people, with the intervention of all the governors (rectors) of the arts of the city; and they governed, with the council of an hundred of the better sort of citizens ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining popular election with participation of corporate bodies (guilds, arts) can distribute legitimacy and expertise across social groups, tempering pure majoritarianism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical enforcement mechanisms to protect the poor/populace from elite abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: The gonfalonier of justice ... shall be bound by the obligation of an oath, and under the penalty, of five hundred pounds, upon the commission of any homicide, to draw forth the standard of justice ... and to cause the bell of the people to be rung ... and all the shops, stores, and warehouses, shall be shut immediately upon the commission of such homicide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutions must include not just declaratory rights but mechanisms and procedures (standards, bells, temporary closures) that allow rapid, visible enforcement to protect vulnerable classes against powerful wrongdoers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutionalization of civic honor and stigma to incentivize behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: To be declared a grandee was rather an infamy than an honour ... they [who live wickedly] shall be recorded in the number of grandees, and accounted as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civic registers, honors, or shames (recording misconduct, public lists) are used historically to shape elite behavior; constitutional design can incorporate reputational sanctions alongside legal ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of public virtue, habits, and mores for constitutional stability
rubrics_metrics.description: The devices on the standards, seals, and coins of the republic ... contained the truest emblem of their government—a lamb pursued by a wolf, with the motto, Peace, riches, and pride; war, poverty, and humility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material institutions alone do not secure stable government; public virtue, manners, and civic habits are essential complements to constitutional structures.
